extracted.intended_audience: litigation counsel, judges, and legal practitioners handling unfair-competition and news-appropriation disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-argument brief seeking equitable relief (injunction) against a rival news service for unfair competition by procuring or using Associated Press news through breaches of confidence and contracts. The page assembles legal standards, factual proof strategies, and authorities to support injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Fighting Ship’ practice as unfair competition
rubrics_metrics.description: When members of a combination place an extra vessel (a 'Fighting Ship') on a berth to match or undercut a non-member's lower fare and thereby keep out the competitor, that coordinated practice is within the prohibition of the Act and is unlawful unfair competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by U.S. v. Hamburg American S. S. Line and similar cases; even if the statute does not name that specific method, particular coordinated methods that restrain trade fall under the general term 'Unfair Competition.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation of news by inducing breach of confidential relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The complainant is entitled to an injunction against appropriation of its news accomplished by inducing the complainant's members or employees to violate the confidential relation under which they receive news and to break their contracts with the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief covers obtaining or permitting a rival to learn of news while in exclusive possession of the complainant, its agents, and members; the remedy is appropriate regardless of the rival's asserted use (tip vs publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Business value of gathered news is protectable property
rubrics_metrics.description: The business value to the complainant — or the news-distributing value of the news which it gathers — is entitled to protection, as long as this value exists, from invasion by a rival agency at any stage and by any method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News gathered by members for distribution constitutes property of the news agency for the benefit of all members from the time of gathering; protection is available through contract, confidence, and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two distinct legal principles: contract and relation of confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection against appropriation of news rests on two distinct principles: contractual rights and confidential relations; there may be a contract without a confidential relation and vice versa, but both can coexist and be invoked together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When both exist the same facts usually apply to both; courts may combine them in one point when seeking relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive rights under bylaws to member-gathered local news
rubrics_metrics.description: By-laws of The Associated Press provide that news gathered by members shall be furnished exclusively to The Associated Press members and the newspapers which they represent; local news gathered by a member is the complainant's property vis-à-vis other members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rival's arrangement with a member made after the member's contract with the complainant is a direct breach and cannot be set up as a defense in equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining news unlawfully is injunctable irrespective of alleged 'tip' use
rubrics_metrics.description: It makes absolutely no difference what use the defendant made of the news; the obtaining of the news was unlawful and subject to injunction even if the rival claims it used information only as a 'tip' and not for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will enjoin the obtaining/inducement itself; attempts to minimize by calling it a 'tip' do not defeat relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducement or procuring of any breach of contract will be enjoined
rubrics_metrics.description: Any inducing or procuring, directly or indirectly, of a breach of contract will be enjoined by equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by numerous authorities cited (e.g., Nashville Ry. Co. v. McConnell; Sperry Co. cases); procurement of breaches gives rise to equitable relief regardless of other asserted defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducement or use of breach of confidential relations will be enjoined
rubrics_metrics.description: Any inducement or use of the breach of a confidential relation respecting a property right, however intangible, will be enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (Peabody v. Norfolk; Simmons Medical Co. v. Simmons; Thrum Co. v. Tiozynski, etc.) demonstrate the established rule that courts protect confidential relations against inducement or exploitation by rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions and uncontroverted facts in affidavits carry decisive weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions by defendant's officers and uncontroverted facts in the record can conclusively establish the complainant's case; negative or vague affidavits of persons claiming ignorance are of little value against positive, detailed rebutting affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where defendants admit arrangements or significant facts, those admissions undermine defenses; lack of counter-affidavits from principal actors is significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting or independent-sourcing assertions do not excuse unlawful obtaining
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's claim that it 'rewrote' a story from a newspaper or relied on independent inquiry does not avoid injunction if the story was obtained by inducing a breach of confidence or contract; the method of obtaining is the critical issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquiries addressed to a party known to have the competing service's information and incorporation of that information indicate lack of true independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-cable/telegraph prohibitions: obtaining dispatches interdicted by governments evidences misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: If a defendant has been prohibited by foreign governments from using cable or telegraph services and yet dispatches correspond to forbidden foreign dispatches, the only inference may be that the defendant relied on the complainant's news — supporting a finding of unlawful appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where nine instances of foreign dispatch appropriation occurred and defendant offered no explanation for eight, the inference of improper use stands uncontested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of 'unclean hands' requires imputable wrongdoing by complainant's principals
rubrics_metrics.description: To bar equitable relief on the ground of unclean hands, the defendant must show misconduct by those responsible for the complainant's policies; sporadic unauthorized acts by subordinate agents, unknown to principals, will not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unauthorized act of an agent does not necessarily impute 'unclean hands' to the principal in equity; authorities (e.g., Vulcan Detinning Co. v. American Can Co.) support this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondeat superior applies differently for complainant and defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine of respondeat superior has no application to the complainant's moral standing (equity's 'unclean hands' inquiry), but it does apply to the defendant so that the defendant is legally responsible for acts of its agents done in the course of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, even if the defendant's president disclaims knowledge, the defendant remains liable for agents' unlawful acts and equitable relief may issue against the defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory/discriminatory pricing as unfair competition
rubrics_metrics.description: A competitor may normally sell below others' prices (even below cost), but selling below cost or discriminating in price in such a manner and for such purpose as will drive a competitor out of business (discriminatory or local reductions intended to eliminate competition) is unlawful unfair competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities include Nash v. U.S.; Standard Oil Co. v. U.S.; Central Lumber Co. v. South Dakota; states have also enacted statutes against this abuse; similar principles apply internationally.
